cards.front: Why must a sample be representative of its population?
cards.back: A **representative** sample mirrors the population, so its results can estimate facts about the population. A poorly chosen sample can mislead even when it is large.
cards.hint: Think about what the sample is for.

cards.front: What makes a simple random sample fair?
cards.back: Every member of the population has an **equal chance** of selection, and chance alone decides who is picked, not the person choosing.

cards.front: Does making a sample bigger remove bias?
cards.back: No. Bias comes from the **method of selection**. A large sample chosen by a faulty method repeats the same error many times.
A **sampling frame** is a list of all the members of the population from which a sample can be drawn.

cards.front: How would you choose a simple random sample of 60 students from a list of 1200?
cards.back: Number the students from 1 to 1200. Generate 60 different random numbers in that range, ignoring repeats. Select the students with those numbers.

cards.front: In systematic sampling, what is $k$ for a population of $N$ and a sample of $n$?
cards.back: $k=\frac{N}{n}$, so take every $k$th member after a **random start**.
cards.hint: Consider how many members lie between each pick.

cards.front: A stratified sample of 80 is needed from 450 Year 10, 350 Year 11 and 200 Year 12 students. How many come from Year 10?
cards.hint: Find the total number of students first.

cards.back: Taking a **random** sample from each group, in proportion to the size of that group.

cards.front: Why is quota sampling not the same as stratified sampling?
cards.back: In quota sampling the **interviewer** chooses who to ask, so chance plays no part and bias can enter. Stratified sampling picks members at random within each group.

cards.front: What is convenience sampling, and why does it bias results?
cards.back: Choosing the members who are **easiest to reach**. Gym users exercise more, so a survey taken outside a gym gives results that are too high.
cards.hint: Think about who is easy to ask.

cards.front: What does bias mean for sample results?
cards.back: A **systematic** error where the selection method favours some members, so results shift in one direction and are consistently wrong.
cards.hint: Think about which way the results move.

cards.back: Bias caused when chosen members do not reply and **differ** from those who do.
A **question worded** so that it encourages one particular answer.

cards.front: What steps reduce bias in data collection?
cards.back: Use a complete **sampling frame**, select members by chance, follow up people who do not reply, and word questions neutrally.
